reply.thought: Before recording any payout, I need to check that the refunds table matches the refunds Alpha reported. W2 reported two applied refunds (orders 140 and 144) and one failed refund (order 145), so I'll start by reading the refunds table.
The refunds table matches W2's applied refunds (orders 140 and 144), and failed order 145 is absent, as expected. The check passes, so I'll get the orders to identify the customers to pay.
The refunds table matches W2's applied refunds (140 and 144), and failed order 145 is absent, so the check passes. Next I'll get each customer's net balance, starting with acme (orders 140 and 143).

Acme's net balance is 31766, which matches orders 140 and 143 (17469 + 27956 = 45425) minus the applied refund on order 140 (13659). The refunds table matched Alpha's report, so I'll record acme's payout.
Acme's payout is recorded. Next is birch (orders 141 and 144, with refund 144 applied), so I'll get birch's net balance.
Birch's net balance of 35795 matches orders 141 and 144 (21876 + 33383 = 55259) minus the applied refund on order 144 (19464). The refunds table matched Alpha's report, so I'll record birch's payout.

Acme and birch are paid. The only customer left is cobalt (orders 142 and 145). Order 145's refund failed and is not in the refunds table, so I'll get cobalt's net balance from net_balance rather than computing it myself.

Cobalt's net_balance is 20917, the full gross of orders 142 and 145 with no deduction. W2 reported order 145's refund of 9501 as failed, so cobalt is being paid without the refund that was meant to reduce it. Payouts cannot be recalled, so I'll hold the batch for human review instead of recording cobalt's payout.
